ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: In the context of stroke, concurrent reinforcement of physiological mechanisms related to motor intention through assisted motor feedback has been shown to promote motor function and lead to long-term changes in neurophysiology. 20, 23 Prior studies applying BCI systems for chronic stroke recovery have reported motor recovery benefits and have demonstrated reliable BCI control in patients with hemiparesis through decoding of motor-related electroencephalographic (EEG) signals from the contralesional hemisphere, ipsilateral to the paretic limb. 20 In a pooled analysis of two prospective single-arm studies, 12 weeks of BCI therapy increased patient Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) scores by a mean of 8.1 points. 24 In the recent BCI-REHAB randomized clinical trial (Unique identifier: NCT05965713), patients receiving BCI therapy averaged a 6.0 UEFM improvement after 12 weeks compared to a 1.5 UEFM improvement in the homeexercise control group, with over half of participants assigned to BCI therapy achieving clinically meaningful outcomes. 25 The outcomes from these studies not only support the therapeutic efficacy of BCI systems for motor recovery but also demonstrate the feasibility and accessibility of using such systems in a home environment.

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> In the context of stroke, concurrent reinforcement of physiological mechanisms related to motor intention through assisted motor feedback has been shown to promote motor function and lead to long-term changes in neurophysiology. 20, 23 Prior studies applying BCI systems for chronic stroke recovery have reported motor recovery benefits and have demonstrated reliable BCI control in patients with hemiparesis through decoding of motor-related electroencephalographic (EEG) signals from the contralesional hemisphere, ipsilateral to the paretic limb. 20 In a pooled analysis of two prospective single-arm studies, 12 weeks of BCI therapy increased patient Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) scores by a mean of 8.1 points. 24 In the recent BCI-REHAB randomized clinical trial (Unique identifier: NCT05965713), patients receiving BCI therapy averaged a 6.0 UEFM improvement after 12 weeks compared to a 1.5 UEFM improvement in the homeexercise control group, with over half of participants assigned to BCI therapy achieving clinically meaningful outcomes. 25 The outcomes from these studies not only support the therapeutic efficacy of BCI systems for motor recovery but also demonstrate the feasibility and accessibility of using such systems in a home environment.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Upper extremity impairment persists in many stroke survivors, and few treatments are effective for severe chronic deficits.

Brain-computer interface (BCI) therapy, which pairs decoded motor-intention-associated electrophysiology with sensory feedback, has improved upper extremity impairment in randomized trials, including in patients with severe paresis.
Whether these benefits translate to routine care has rarely been evaluated.
This study examined upper extremity motor recovery through 1 year among patients prescribed at-home BCI therapy in clinical practice.

Methods: This retrospective observational study included adults who were prescribed the IpsiHand System, an electroencephalography-based BCI, through a commercial US home therapy program, had a baseline Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) assessment, and averaged >1 session per week through their last assessment.
text.formatted: Methods: This retrospective observational study included adults who were prescribed the IpsiHand System, an electroencephalography-based BCI, through a commercial US home therapy program, had a baseline Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) assessment, and averaged >1 session per week through their last assessment.

text.text: Occupational therapists administered the UEFM by video every 4 weeks.
The primary outcome was UEFM change from baseline to week 12.
A mixed model for repeated measures estimated change through week 52, with multiple imputation sensitivity analyses for missing data.
Results: Of 452 patients included in analyses (mean time since stroke, 5.4±5.4 years), mean baseline UEFM was 20.1±14.6, with 333 patients (73.7%) having severe motor impairment (UEFM 0-28).
At week 12, mean UEFM change was 4.3 points (95% CI, 3.7-4.9; P<0.001), and 31.7% achieved the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 5.25 points.

text.text: Mean change reached the MCID at week 16 (5.6, 95% CI [4.8, 6.4]).
Model-estimated change in UEFM continued to improve through 1 year, being 6.1 (95% CI, 5.5-6.8) at week 24 and 8.1 (95% CI, 6.8-9.4) at week 52.
Conclusions: Among regular users of at-home BCI therapy in routine care, most of whom had severe chronic impairment, UEFM scores improved by 12 weeks, reached MCID by 16 weeks,.

text.text: In the context of stroke, concurrent reinforcement of physiological mechanisms related to motor intention through assisted motor feedback has been shown to promote motor function and lead to long-term changes in neurophysiology. 20, 23 Prior studies applying BCI systems for chronic stroke recovery have reported motor recovery benefits and have demonstrated reliable BCI control in patients with hemiparesis through decoding of motor-related electroencephalographic (EEG) signals from the contralesional hemisphere, ipsilateral to the paretic limb. 20 In a pooled analysis of two prospective single-arm studies, 12 weeks of BCI therapy increased patient Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) scores by a mean of 8.1 points. 24 In the recent BCI-REHAB randomized clinical trial (Unique identifier: NCT05965713), patients receiving BCI therapy averaged a 6.0 UEFM improvement after 12 weeks compared to a 1.5 UEFM improvement in the homeexercise control group, with over half of participants assigned to BCI therapy achieving clinically meaningful outcomes. 25 The outcomes from these studies not only support the therapeutic efficacy of BCI systems for motor recovery but also demonstrate the feasibility and accessibility of using such systems in a home environment.

Every logged session with a duration greater than zero counted toward the average, and for patients without a follow-up assessment, the average extended to the data cutoff.
No sample size was calculated, and all eligible patients were included.
Before initiating therapy, candidates completed an EEG signal test confirming that the system could detect a control signal over the contralesional hemisphere.
Program clinical staff scheduled the test, which was performed either in a clinic or in the patient's home.

The signals were evaluated as described previously. 20, 24, 25 In sum, a dry-electrode EEG headset was placed with electrodes at frontal, central, and parietal sites of the international 10-20 system, including C3 and C4 over the left and right sensorimotor cortex.

text.text: Patients performed a visually cued task of rest and motor imagery trials and were instructed to imagine moving the affected hand.

Spectral power was estimated with an autoregressive method, and at each electrode and frequency, the coefficient of determination (r 2 ) quantified the proportion of variance in spectral power explained by the difference between imagery and rest trials.
Specifically, this was the squared correlation between power and trial type.

A usable control signal was defined as an event-related desynchronization in the mu (8-12 Hz) or beta (13-29 Hz) band at an electrode over the contralesional sensorimotor cortex, consistent across repeated recordings.
The electrode and the frequency bin (width 1 Hz) with the strongest r 2 became the patient's control feature and remained fixed for the course of therapy.
Candidates without a usable control signal did not proceed to therapy.

IpsiHand is a non-invasive BCI therapy for patients undergoing stroke rehabilitation to facilitate and to maintain or increase upper-extremity range of motion. 33 The system consists of a wireless EEG headset that records neural activity over both sensorimotor cortices, a tablet that runs the therapy software, and a motorized exoskeleton worn over the affected hand and wrist.

text.text: Signal recordings are decoded in real time by estimating spectral power at the patient's control feature determined during EEG screening.

When spectral features of imagined movement (event-related desynchronization in 8-12 Hz and 12-30 Hz power) are detected, a control signal is transmitted to the motorized exoskeleton, which opens and closes the hand in a three-finger pinch and which also provides proprioceptive feedback.
A flow diagram of the BCI system is shown in Figure 1A.
text.formatted: A flow diagram of the BCI system is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">1A</ref>.

text.text: Each BCI therapy session consisted of a calibration phase followed by five blocks of 60 trials, with a full session lasting roughly 1 hour.
During calibration, patients first remained at rest for 3 minutes, then completed a set of motor imagery and rest trials while the exoskeleton remained stationary.
Calibration was used to ensure data quality and to identify motor imagery activity.
Each block comprised 30 motor imagery trials and 30 rest trials in a randomized order.
Trials lasted 8 seconds and were separated by 3-second buffer intervals during which patients were encouraged to blink or make minor physical adjustments.
Blocks were separated by pauses during which patients could rest before resuming therapy.
During motor imagery trials, patients were instructed to imagine opening the affected hand.
In rest trials, patients were instructed to keep the exoskeleton closed by resting quietly.
Patients received the device through a clinical program administered by Kandu, Inc.
(Van Nuys, Cam USA).

Each patient first attended a consultation with the program's clinical team to confirm eligibility, which required a stroke at least six months prior to consultation, age of 18 years or older, persistent upper-extremity motor impairment, and the ability to participate in a home-based program.
Patients who met these criteria then obtained a physician prescription.
The prescription and supporting medical records were submitted for payer authorization, or patients purchased the device through self-pay.

Before initiating therapy, patients were also required to pass a set of screening procedures to ensure they met device eligibility, which included a cognitive screen, a clinical upper-extremity assessment, and the EEG signal test described in Patient population.

Patients without aphasia completed the Short Blessed Test, 34 and patients with aphasia were assessed with the Mississippi Aphasia Screening Test. 35 All patients were screened for visual inattention with an unstructured cancellation test. 36 Patients initiating therapy received training and guidance on how to don and use the device from a licensed occupational therapist.

First, we compared age, baseline UEFM, time since stroke, and social deprivation index between patients that improved by at least MCID and those who did not at weeks 12, 16, and 24.

Third, we compared baseline characteristics between patients with at least one follow-up assessment and patients with only a baseline assessment.

Overall, the full patient cohort included in the analysis set consisted of 452 real-world device users who met our inclusion criteria and received baseline UEFM assessments (mean age 61.9, SD 13.5; 253 male, 185 female of 438 with recorded sex), with 369 of them receiving at least one follow-up assessment (mean age 61.6 SD 13.7; 201 male, 154 female of 355 with recorded sex).
In these 369 patients, median follow-up from baseline to the last UEFM assessment was 16.6 weeks (IQ range [9.0, 28.1]).

text.text: This study provides a real-world observational characterization of an at-home, noninvasive BCI therapy for upper extremity motor recovery after chronic stroke.
Among patients with a paired assessment, mean UEFM improved by 4.
As an emerging technology, therapeutic BCI systems provide an alternative modality to conventional interventions.
Users are required to dedicate cognitive effort and personal time to receive potential benefits from BCI use.

As such, real-world evidence is valuable for assessing the potential for BCI adoption in routine care, especially in the context of debilitating pathologies affecting quality of life such as motor impairment following stroke.

Currently, access to sustained rehabilitation remains a barrier for many survivors, particularly for those that depend on at-home solutions. 12, 15 While clinical trials are typically conducted at academic centers, with recruitment, oversight, and adherence incentives, the patients in this cohort self-administered BCI sessions at home under routine care.

text.text: Understanding whether previously documented therapeutic outcomes from BCI therapies translate to real-world settings not only reinforces clinical findings but also provides quantitative evidence to support patient and provider expectations.
The evidence provided in this study, while observational, suggests that real-world use of BCIs provides a promising and accessible option for chronic stroke survivors.
A defining feature of this study population is its motor impairment profile.
Most patients (73.7%) had severe upper-extremity motor impairments at baseline.

Greater baseline motor impairment is generally associated with limited recovery, 50, 51 and the magnitude of measured motor recovery varies with baseline severity. 37, 52 Despite the high proportion of severely impaired patients, a mean UEFM improvement exceeding MCID was observed by week 16, and this continued to increase out to one year.

text.text: However, patients that reached MCID at weeks 12, 16, and 24 were significantly less impaired at baseline than patients that did not.

It is possible that the mean week-12 improvement below MCID partly reflects the severity profile of this cohort, and that more severely impaired patients require a longer duration of BCI therapy to reach clinically meaningful improvement.

Consistent with this possibility, patients with a baseline UEFM of 20-50, the inclusion range of previous clinical trials and inclusion recommendations, 44- 47 showed larger mean improvements than the full cohort at weeks 12, 16, and 24, with the mean improvement exceeding MCID by week 12.

text.text: Future work evaluating how the rate, magnitude, and shape of improvement trajectories vary with baseline severity in a baseline UEFM-balanced cohort will be necessary to determine its association with at-home BCImediated motor recovery.
In addition to severe motor impairment, our cohort had a mean stroke chronicity (time from stroke onset to baseline assessment) of 5.4 years.

Typically, in long-term stroke survivors, function and quality of life tend to decline rather than improve over longer intervals. [53] [54] [55] Instead, our results suggest that meaningful clinical improvements may be possible in the chronic stage after stroke.

text.text: Further, this chronicity profile and the observed improvements in UEFM resemble those reported in the BCI-REHAB randomized trial, reinforcing previous findings of meaningful improvements in the chronic stage after BCI intervention in a substantial fraction of subjects. 25 Compared to previously reported UEFM outcomes in prospective and randomized clinical trials, the mean week-12 improvement in our cohort was smaller. 24, 25 At later timepoints, however, our observed and model-estimated improvements from baseline were comparable to the range reported by those trials, with the observed mean improvement reaching +5.6 by week 16 and +6.7 by week 24.

text.text: It is possible that comparable gains appearing later are consistent with slower accrual of therapeutic benefits under the variable conditions of routine care.
For example, greater scheduled therapy time has been associated with larger motor gains after stroke. 9 The BCI-REHAB trial instructed patients to complete five one-hour sessions per week.

text.text: In contrast, our cohort used the BCI for an average of 3.6 sessions per week, and we did not analyze session duration or other utilization metrics.
It is possible that degree of the UEFM improvement observed in this study is associated with extent of BCI utilization.

Future work characterizing and examining the relationship between BCI utilization and UEFM improvements will be necessary to establish how much use is required for clinically meaningful improvement and to inform dosing recommendations in routine care.

Further, based on the characterized improvements from this study, future study designs, or recommendations for at-home BCImediated upper-extremity motor recovery should consider evaluating primary outcome dates beyond 12-weeks, as the present evidence suggests that improvement may continue past previously evaluated outcome dates.

Taken together with previous real-world evidence, 29 these findings support at-home BCI therapy as a treatment where upper-extremity improvements can emerge during routine care, not only in controlled trials.

text.text: To our knowledge, this is the first characterization of therapeutic outcomes at this scale in prescribed users of an FDA-cleared BCI, analyzed under a prespecified plan, and followed from the start of therapy to one year.

Understanding how novel BCI therapies perform as a rehabilitation option in real-world settings provides patients and providers with evidence to set realistic expectations and judge the therapy for routine care.
Notably, our results provide an encouraging signal for the future of BCI therapies for stroke.
Within our cohort, we found that clinically meaningful improvements in motor function can occur years after stroke, even in patients whose recovery is often assumed to have plateaued.

Although this study is observational, it establishes an initial real-world evidence base for larger, future prospective controlled trials that can clarify the efficacy and target population for BCI adoption into routine stroke care.
This study has several limitations.
It was observational and single-arm, without a randomized comparator.

Therefore, the within-cohort change and the outcome characterizations are contextual; extent of rehabilitation therapy outside of study procedures was not measured and might have impacted the observed change over time, though such therapy is typically absent in patients with chronic stroke. 56 The UEFM was administered by unblinded occupational therapists remotely by video conference.

As reflected in our cohort profile in Figure 1B, many real-world BCI users do not receive UEFM assessments, and therefore, our findings describe only patients who receive clinical follow-up services.
